Part I
第一章　最后的药典
1　The Last Pharmacopeia
1505年夏，以弘治（意为“宏大治理”）为年号的明朝皇帝朱祐樘患病，年仅三十五岁便去世了。朝中要员把这位年轻皇帝的早逝归咎于热性药物——这类药本绝不该用来治疗暑热引发的疾病。他们指控太医院院使刘文泰与司礼监太监张瑜犯下弑君之罪。
In the summer of 1505, Zhu Youcheng, the emperor of Ming China under the reign name of
Hongzhi

(Grand Governance), became ill and died at thirty-five. Leading officials attributed the young emperor’s premature death to hot-natured drugs that should never have been prescribed to treat diseases arising from summer heat. They blamed Liu Wentai, superintendent of the Imperial Academy of Medicine, and Zhang Yu, the chief palace eunuch, for the crime of regicide.
这一指控的讽刺之处在于，刘、张二人不久前才刚刚宣称在药学领域取得了一项重大成就。已故的弘治皇帝一向雅好医术，时常向贫民施药。
1503年，皇帝命刘文泰与张瑜率领一批宫廷医官编纂一部新的本草药典。两年后，这个团队向御前呈上一部装帧精美、附图丰富的手稿，收载药物1,815种，卷首还冠有皇帝亲撰的短序，题为《御制本草品汇精要》（下称《品汇精要》）。几个月后，弘治帝猝然驾崩，刘、张二人随即失势。这部药典被封存起来，从未流出宫外。
编者说明：《名山藏》卷十九记“上好医药，常以剂赐臣民”，受赠者称臣民，未限定为贫民；底本所据具体页叶尚未亲见。

The irony in this accusation lies in the fact that Liu and Zhang had only recently claimed a great accomplishment in the field of pharmacy. The late Hongzhi emperor had always cherished the art of medicine, frequently donating medications to the poor.

In 1503, the emperor asked Liu and Zhang to compile a new bencao pharmacopeia with a team of palace physicians. Two years later, the team presented the throne with a beautifully illustrated manuscript that documented 1,815 kinds of materia medica, further adorned with a short preface by the emperor himself, under the title
Yuzhi Bencao pinhui jingyao (Imperially Commissioned, Essentials of Assorted and Collected Materia Medica
; hereafter
Essentials
). A few months later, Liu and Zhang fell from grace following the sudden passing of Hongzhi. The pharmacopeia was sealed off and never distributed outside the palace.
Editor's note (Chinese): 《名山藏》卷十九记“上好医药，常以剂赐臣民”，受赠者称臣民，未限定为贫民；底本所据具体页叶尚未亲见。
在士大夫圈子里，关于刘文泰的种种故事在整个16世纪流传不绝。一则流行的轶事称，刘文泰其实还对1487年成化帝（弘治之父）之死负有责任。故事说，刘侥幸逃脱重罚之后便向政敌发难，逼迫一位德高望重的大臣致仕。
更多故事把弘治帝描绘成临终时渴求饮水、因热盛而鼻血直流，刘文泰却拒绝让他喝水。还有人追问，刘文泰与张瑜究竟是如何逃过死罪的——又或者，是不是皇帝遗孀因信赖二人多年侍奉而受其蒙蔽，出面干预，才使他们免于治罪？
弘治药典的编纂过程同样充满不谐：刘文泰请求两位翰林院学士为医官“校书”，内阁却视之为侮辱。他们主张，士人的本分在于“论思”国政，因此拒绝与宫廷医官共事。

In scholar-official circles, stories about Liu Wentai lingered throughout the sixteenth century. One popular anecdote claimed that Liu was in fact also responsible for the death of the Chenghua emperor (Hongzhi’s father) back in 1487. Having narrowly escaped severe punishment, so the story goes, Liu lashed out against his foes, forcing a well-respected minister to retire.

More stories portrayed the Hongzhi emperor on his deathbed begging for water, his nose bleeding from excessive heat, with Liu refusing to let him drink. Another questioned how Liu and Zhang managed to escape the death penalty—or, might it have been the emperor’s widow, deceived by her trust in Liu and Zhang’s long-time service, who intervened and exonerated them?

The making of the Hongzhi pharmacopeia, too, was replete with dissonance: when Liu Wentai requested the help of two Hanlin academicians to serve as “proofreaders,” the grand secretariat took it as an insult. Arguing that a scholar’s proper job was the “discussion and deliberation” (
lunsi
) of state policy, they refused to work with the palace physicians.
这场围绕皇帝之死的分裂性争斗，为我们理解16世纪本草作为知识领域的迅速转型提供了关键背景。这些故事把刘文泰描绘成恶人，恰与嘉靖（1522—1566）与万历（1572—1620）两朝漫长的继统争议所激起的紧张气氛相合。士大夫希望以道德学问匡正公共事务，因而感到有责任对皇室的健康与维护问题表明立场。这些耸人听闻的轶事，源于他们的恐惧：只需一个庸医——或者更糟，一个蓄意作恶之人——便足以动摇“国本”。
与此同时，医学专家与宦官一有机会便迅速反击。刘文泰等人在弘治药典的序中，对那位不屑与自己共事的士大夫作了含蓄的讥刺。“旧本之文而志士鸿儒则能斟酌其是非，”刘文泰等人写道；而他的新本，“虽初学庸材不待参详而即悟”。
在这番自谦的语调背后，是一种难以忽视的桀骜。

This divisive battle over an emperor’s death offers us a crucial context for understanding the rapid transformation of bencao as a field of knowledge during the sixteenth century. By casting Liu in an unholy light, the tales fit into the contentious mood stoked by later controversies over imperial succession during the long Jiajing (1522–66) and Wanli (1572–1620) reigns. Scholar-officials, seeking to rectify public affairs with their moral learning, felt compelled to weigh in on issues pertaining to the health and maintenance of the imperial family. The sensational anecdotes emerged out of their fear that it took only one incompetent physician—or even worse, an intentionally malignant person—to shake the “root of the State” (
guoben

Medical experts and eunuchs, meanwhile, were quick to punch back whenever they had a chance. In his preface to the Hongzhi pharmacopeia, Liu Wentai took a subtle jab at the scholar-official who would not deign to work with him. “The old bencao is intelligible only to virtuous gentlemen and erudite scholars,” noted Liu, whereas his text would be “easy to understand by novices and mediocre persons without much hard thinking.”
Hiding behind his self-deprecating tones is a defiance that is hard to miss.

就短期而言，一部国家敕修药典的命运，被明代政体中士大夫与技术专家之间的政治僵局断送了。本章则提供另一种叙事，转而考察这些药物物性的“总览”在文本流传与接受上的较长轨迹。我认为，权威的去中心化早在11世纪便已充分展开，尽管北宋朝廷确实敕修过不止一部本草药典。按时间顺序考察本草作为一个探究领域，有三种趋势格外突出。第一，宋代国家无法对这些繁复文本的流传施加多少控制。各类作者独立于朝廷，对官方版本加以改动，并通过写本或新近可用的印刷技术推广自己的作品。

In the short term, the fate of a state-commissioned pharmacopeia was doomed by the political impasse between scholar-officials and technical experts in the Ming polity. In this chapter, I offer a different narrative that examines instead the longer trajectory of textual transmission and reception for these “pandects” of pharmaceutical objecthood. I argue that the decentralization of authority had already been well under way since the eleventh century, when the Northern Song court did commission multiple bencao pharmacopeias. Proceeding chronologically, three trends stand out when we examine bencao as a field of inquiry. First, the Song state could not exert much control over these elaborate texts in transmission. A variety of authors, acting independently of the imperial court, made changes to the official edition and promoted their work through the manuscript or the newly available technology of printing.

第二，金元时期（13至14世纪）的重大医学创新，促使医家以宇宙论的、系统化的术语解释药理作用。这些作者不再措意于药典的博学，转而试图建立一套由关联性宇宙论支撑的实用药学课程。他们的努力又因当时商业出版者影响力的上升而得到加强。最后，地方官刻——明代书籍文化的一大标志——使繁复的宋代药典自15世纪中叶起得以广泛印行。其结果是，数量空前的大批文本涌现出来，试图把宇宙论药理学与药典结合起来，创造出新的话语与文本类型。明代读者开始通过书本学习药学，在彼此之间形成不再依赖朝廷的文本共同体。

Second, major medical innovations during the Jin-Yuan period (thirteenth through fourteenth centuries) inspired physicians to explain pharmacological action in cosmic, systematic terms. Turning away from the pharmacopeia’s erudition, these authors aimed instead to create a practical curriculum of pharmacy informed by correlative cosmology. Their efforts were augmented by the rising influence of commercial publishers at that time. Lastly, regional official publishing—a hallmark of Ming book culture—made the elaborate Song pharmacopeia widely available in print from the mid-fifteenth century. As a result, an unprecedented number of texts emerged that attempted to
integrate
cosmic pharmacology with the pharmacopeia, creating new discourses and textual genres. Ming readers came to learn pharmacy by the book, creating
textual communities
among themselves that no longer depended on the imperial court.
凭借这一从书籍史获得的洞见，我们可以重新把李时珍的《本草纲目》视为16世纪书籍文化的一种特殊产物。一方面，李时珍受益于本草文本及其他重要文献的广泛印行。另一方面，我们也应看到，李时珍竟敢设想自己能够编纂一部新药典，这是何等不寻常——如前所述，这项事业在16世纪初作为政治工程已然受挫。最终，使李时珍这部巨著取得持久成功的，并非皇家赞助，而是博学读者的需求。
Armed with this insight drawn from book history, we can revisit Li Shizhen’s
Bencao gangmu

as a peculiar product of sixteenth-century book culture. On the one hand, Li Shizhen benefited from the widespread availability of bencao texts and other important sources in print. On the other hand, we should also see how unusual it was for Li Shizhen to presume that he could make a new pharmacopeia that, as we have seen, fell short as a political project in the early sixteenth century. In the end, it was not imperial patronage that made Li Shizhen’s magnum opus a lasting success, but the demands of learned readers.
宋元明之际药典的延续
The Persistence of Pharmacopeias during the Song-Yuan-Ming Transition
早在印刷术出现之前，早期本草的内容便已通过写本广为流传。然而，收藏于宫廷档案的唐代药典原本由若干部分组成，按不同的分析类型划分：注文、地方呈报与图。图像部分几乎从未传出京城，而文本片段则流动得远为自由。陶弘景5世纪的注本与唐本草都西传至敦煌、吐鲁番，东传至日本平安朝。

Even prior to the advent of printing, the content of early bencao was transmitted widely in manuscript copies. The original Tang pharmacopeia housed at the court archive, however, consisted of multiple parts divided by different kinds of analysis: commentaries, local reports, and illustrations. The pictorial component was hardly seen beyond the capital city, whereas fragments of text traveled much more freely. Both Tao Hongjing’s fifth-century commentaries and the Tang bencao circulated as far as Dunhuang and Turfan to the west, and Hei’an Japan to the east.

到了11世纪，宋廷臣僚沿袭唐的先例，编成一部由两部分组成的药典：增补的注文，以及地方呈报的汇编（图经，意为“地图指南”）。两部分由不同的团队主持，在五年之内（1057—1061）完成，篇幅远较唐代版本为多。尽管朝廷命两部分各以雕版印行并分发至各地官署，它们使用起来却极为不便。地方读者很快便开始依据官方药典自行编纂节要与注本。例如，一位名叫陈承的医者（约活动于1086—1110年）把官方文本两编中的相关章节合为一书，最终因此在太医局谋得一个令人羡慕的职位。
又如，寇宗奭（约活动于1111—1117年）在今日湖南一带担任小官，自撰注本以“衍义”官方药典。他后来升任京城的“辨验药材”，其亲属也将他的本草注本付梓推广。
从这些例子可以看出，本草如何成为一个医者与士大夫可以自由交谈的共同兴趣领域，而本草学上的成就也能带来仕途上的升迁。
Come the eleventh century, Song courtiers followed the Tang precedent to create a two-part pharmacopeia: an expanded commentary and a compilation of local reports (
tujing

, or “map guides”). Headed by separate teams, the two parts were completed within five years (1057–61) and were much longer compared to the Tang version. Although the court commissioned each part to be reproduced in woodblock print and distributed to local offices, they proved unwieldy to use. Local readers soon started to compile their own digests and commentaries based on the official pharmacopeia. For example, a physician named Chen Cheng (fl. 1086–1110) produced a composite bencao by combining relevant sections in each part of the official text, which eventually earned him a desirable post in the imperial medical administration.
Similarly, Kou Zongshi (fl. 1111–17), a minor official stationed in later-day Hunan, compiled his own commentary to “propagate the meanings” (
yanyi
) of the official pharmacopeia. He was later promoted to the “purveyor and inspector of materia medica” (
bianyan yaocai
) in the capital city, and his relatives promoted his bencao commentaries in print as well.

From these examples, we see how bencao became a field of common interest in which physicians and scholar-officials could freely converse, and accomplishment in bencao scholarship could lead to promotions in officialdom.

12世纪初，杭州地方官赞助刊刻了一部新的本草写本。杭州无人知晓作者唐慎微的来历，却都对这部著作印象深刻：它不仅合并了官方药典的两个部分，还从广泛的医学与文学文献中增补了五百种新药。这部1108年的刻本以当时的年号称作《大观本草》，因此在许多方面都超过了宋代的官方药典。徽宗一向热衷于医事，命宫廷医官迅速编出一部经官方修订的新版，结果更名为《政和本草》（1116年新版颁行时的年号）。此书问世后，两编本的宋代官方药典逐渐停止流通，直到20世纪，学者才为历史研究把两部分分别重构出来。
1127年，宋政权在北方女真人的攻击下崩溃，一位皇子退往南方，在杭州巩固统治。女真金朝与南宋之间的敌对与封锁，意外地造成唐慎微本草两种略有差异的版本南北分隔。

In the early 1100s, the local administrator of Hangzhou sponsored the printing of a new bencao manuscript. No one in Hangzhou knew anything about the author, Tang Shenwei, and yet they were impressed by his work, which not only combined the two-part official pharmacopeia but also included five hundred new entries of materia medica culled from a wide range of medical and literary sources. This 1108 print edition, known as the
Daguan bencao

after the current reign title, thus surpassed the Song official pharmacopeia in many ways. Ever enthusiastic about medical matters, Emperor Huizong ordered court physicians to quickly produce a new edition with official revisions. The result was rebranded as the
Zhenghe bencao

(the reign name when the new edition was released in 1116). Following its appearance, the two-part Song official pharmacopeia gradually ceased to circulate, and only in the twentieth century did scholars reconstruct each part for historical research.

In 1127, the Song regime fell to Jurchen attacks from the north, and one prince retreated to the south, consolidating his rule in Hangzhou. The resulting hostility and blockade between the Jurchen Jin dynasty and the Southern Song resulted in the unintended separation of two slightly different editions of Tang Shenwei’s bencao.
在南北两地，都出现了有助于揭示唐慎微身份的新材料。一则南方资料透露，唐慎微是一位在中国西部行医的医生，一位武官曾延请他到成都居住。

在北方，宇文虚中（1079—1146）——一位作为国使被金人扣留的宋朝老臣——在囚禁中为《政和本草》写了一篇短跋。跋中称，他亲眼目睹唐慎微在成都逗留期间为其父治病，效验如神。宇文虚中形容唐慎微“貌寝陋，举措语言朴讷”，并解释说，他为士人治病不收钱财，只求得到含有医药内容的文本。宇文虚中暗示，正因如此，唐慎微才得以汇集足够多的秘方与珍稀文本，编成一部在博学上超过官方药典的本草。在这个故事里，唐慎微成了宇文虚中追忆宋代文教风流时一个理想化的象征。

In both south and north, new information emerged to shed light on Tang Shenwei’s identity. A southern source revealed that Tang Shenwei was a physician living and practicing in West China, and that a military official had recruited him to live in Chengdu.
In the north, Yuwen Xuzhong (1079–1146), a veteran Song official imprisoned by the Jurchens as a state emissary, wrote a short epigraph to the
Zhenghe bencao

during his captivity. In it, Yuwen claimed to have witnessed Tang Shenwei treat his father with miraculous efficacy during Tang’s stay in Chengdu. Describing Tang as a man “ugly in appearance and slow in demeanor and speech,” Yuwen explained that he treated literati not for money, but instead asked for texts with medical content. In so doing, Yuwen hinted, Tang was able to gather enough secret recipes and rare texts to compile a bencao that surpassed the official pharmacopeia in erudition. In this story, Tang Shenwei became an idealized symbol in Yuwen’s melancholy reminiscence of literary culture in Song times.
出版记录显示，12世纪与13世纪大部分时间里南北文化的对峙，实际上延续了本草药典的权威。在南方，高宗（1127—1162年在位）刚在杭州安顿下来，便敕修了一部新药典。仿佛是350年后刘文泰争议的预演，这部南宋本草虽告完成，却因官员与太医院长官之间的争执而从未获得公开认可。
宫廷医官仍继续依据宋代药典选拔新人。在笔试中，考生须辨认某些药材，并依据本草所载各味药的属性组方。有趣的是，宫廷医官抱怨说，应试合格者大多来自京城附近，这说明这些繁复文本的流通范围大概并不很远。
相反，药典的“俗刻”往往把原本一千六百余页的篇幅大幅删削，出现在中国东南日益成长的出版业中。士大夫为此感到有责任出资另刻，以纠正这些刻本的错误——这一模式我们将在15世纪末至16世纪初再次看到。

Publishing records suggest that the north-south cultural rivalry during much of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries in fact perpetuated the authority of bencao pharmacopeias. In the south, soon after installing himself in Hangzhou, the Gaozong emperor (r. 1127–62) commissioned a new pharmacopeia. In a pattern foreshadowing the Liu Wentai controversy 350 years later, the Southern Song bencao was completed but never gained public endorsement due to the bickering between officials and the chief palace physician.

Palace physicians continued to refer to the Song pharmacopeia to recruit new personnel. In written examinations, candidates were asked to identify certain kinds of materia medica and construct formulas based on the properties of each ingredient as documented in the bencao. Interestingly, court physicians complained that most qualifying candidates for the exams hailed from the vicinity of the capital, indicating that the circulation of these elaborate texts probably did not go very far.
Instead, “vulgar imprints” (
suke

) of the pharmacopeia, often greatly truncated from its original length of over 1,600 pages, appeared in the growing publishing sectors in Southeast China. In response, civil officials felt compelled to fund additional editions to correct these imprints’ errors, a pattern that we shall also see repeat in the late fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries.
在北方，一部重要的《政和本草》于1249年在平阳府问世。平阳府是晋南的文教与出版中心（见地图0.1）。出版者张存惠延请能工巧匠，为每一种药物的描述配上精美的木刻插图，其中包括三幅整页的海盐与岩盐场图（后者为晋南特产）。金朝刚刚被蒙古人征服之际，两位显要的士人官员为该书作序，申明本草作为文化资产的核心地位。
然而，中国士人并非本草唯一的倡导者：在金朝统治的最后几十年里，唐慎微本草的一个略有改动的版本被收入《道藏》。这是一项由全真道广泛流行所推动的宏伟工程。此后，本草一直是道教典籍的一部分，后世许多读者正是通过道教关系才得以接触到它们。
In the north, an important edition of
Zhenghe bencao

came out in 1249 in the Pingyang Prefecture, a center of literary culture and publishing in southern Shanxi (see map 0.1). The publisher, Zhang Cunhui, recruited skillful artisans to produce beautiful woodcut illustrations that accompanied the description of every drug, including three full-page illustrations of sea salt and rock salt yards (the latter native to that part of Shanxi). Two prominent literati officials wrote prefaces for the text, stating the centrality of bencao as a cultural asset, at a time when the Jin regime in turn had just been conquered by the Mongols.
The Chinese literati were, however, not the only advocates for bencao: in the last decades of Jin rule, a slightly altered version of Tang Shenwei’s pharmacopeia appeared in the
Daoist Canon

, a monumental undertaking fueled by the widespread popularity of Quanzhen Daoism. Bencao remained thereafter part of the Daoist corpus, and many readers later got access to them via Daoist connections.
总而言之，在北宋灭亡后南北分治的150年间，本草药典在北方与南方都保持了它的吸引力与声望。参与保存、传递与挪用本草的众多行动者，跨越了政治分野与宗教信仰。蒙古灭南宋后，元朝曾在忽必烈治下短暂考虑过编修一部新本草，但由此产生的文本即使曾经存在，也早已失传。
撇开偶然因素不谈，注意力从药典编纂上的转移，或许也与医学之学的重心变化有关。

To sum up, for 150 years of divided rule after the Northern Song’s demise, the bencao pharmacopeia retained its appeal and prestige in both the north and south. The multitude of actors involved in saving, transmitting, and appropriating bencao crossed political divisions and religious creeds. After the Mongol conquest of the Southern Song, the Yuan dynasty briefly entertained the idea of a new bencao under the rule of Kublai Khan, but the resulting text, if it ever existed, is long lost.
Contingencies aside, the shift of attention away from pharmacopeia-making may also have had to do with changing priorities in medical learning.
宇宙论药理学的兴起
The Rise of Cosmic Pharmacology
唐宋药典规模宏大、内容庞杂，本不是为当时的普通医者而作。12世纪，当卷帙浩繁的药典仍在精英士人圈中可见之际，一种新型药理学经由几位医家的著述与教学而崭露头角。所谓“金元诸师”之所以成名，不仅在于他们阐明单味药能治什么病，更在于说明其为何能治，以及透彻理解药理学如何能使医疗实践焕发生机。他们的成功还依赖于创造新的文本类型，而这些类型在日益扩张的印刷文化中极为流行。

Monumental in scale and eclectic in content, the Tang and Song pharmacopeias were not intended for the average medical practitioner of the day. During the twelfth century, when the extensive pharmacopeias remained visible among elite literati circles, a new type of pharmacology rose to prominence via the writing and teaching of a few master physicians. The so-called Masters of Jin-Yuan made their fame by articulating not
what
individual drugs could cure, but also
why

they did so, and in what ways medical practices could be invigorated by a thorough understanding of pharmacology. Their success also depended on inventing new textual genres that proved extremely successful in an expanding culture of print.

这种新药理学的产物之一，是一部题为《珍珠囊药性赋》的短篇文本，托名于张元素（1151—1234）。与收药一千七百余种的宋代药典相比，《珍珠囊》只选取200至300种常用药，并按其“性”分为寒、热、温、平四类。此类描述虽已见于本草传统，唐宋药典却未曾对这些属性作出系统解释，也未按药理作用对药物进行分类。《珍珠囊》还极易诵读：每味药只有一句描述，不引前人文献，每两句成一联，与下一联押韵。此书属于当时兴起的启蒙读物与记忆指南一类——这一现象与科举在通俗文化中的上升有关。《珍珠囊》的各种改编本作为药学入门书，一直流行到20世纪初。
One product of this new pharmacology is a short text titled
Pearl Pouch and Rhymes on the Nature of Drugs (Zhenzhu nang yaoxing fu
), attributed to Zhang Yuansu (1151–1234). In contrast to the Song pharmacopeia’s coverage of more than 1,700 drugs,
Pearl Pouch
selects only 200–300 common drugs, and divides them into four groups by their “nature” (
xing

) as cold, hot, warm, or “flat.” Although such descriptions existed in the bencao tradition, the Tang and Song pharmacopeias did not offer a systematic explanation of these properties, nor did they classify drugs by their pharmacological action.
Pearl Pouch

is also very easy to read: Each drug gets a one-sentence description with no reference to previous literature, and every two sentences form a couplet that rhymes with the next pair. This text belongs to the rising genre of primers and mnemonic guides—a phenomenon linked to the ascendance of the civil service examina- tion in popular culture at the time. Various renditions of
Pearl Pouch
would remain popular as an introductory text on pharmacology well into the early twentieth century.
另一部短篇文本托名于李杲（1180—1251），阐述了更为具体的宇宙论药理学。李杲是一位受过良好教育的医者，其临床强调使用温补之品；他亲历蒙古对华北的征服，所教医学重视缓解饥困与忧苦所致之病。这篇药学短论提出，寒、热、温、平（凉）不只是药理作用的感觉，而是四时的“法象”，即天在不同阴阳配置下的显现（史家乌尔丽克·翁舒尔德把这一理论译为一种“生热之性”）。
同样，药味虽也见于药典记载，却未被系统化，此时则被标准化，以与构成大地的五行相配。于是，一幅兼括天地的宇宙图景，涵盖了这些变量的无穷组合，而这些组合又对应不同的时令周期与药理作用。运用这一模型，医家的诊断与处方便成为一个复杂的推理过程，须把时间、地点、病位、病人体质以及单味药之性统统考虑在内（见表1.1）。换言之，做一名良医，就要像占卜者那样解读大宇宙与小宇宙的隐秘机制。

Another short text, attributed to Li Gao (1180–1251), articulates a more specific theory of cosmic pharmacology. A well-educated physician whose practice emphasized the use of warming tonics, Li witnessed the Mongol conquest of northern China and taught medicine that emphasized alleviating diseases caused by hunger and distress. The short treatise on pharmacology proposes seeing cold, hot, warm, and flat (cool) as not mere sensations of pharmacological action, but “regular images” (
faxiang
) of the four seasons, or different yin/ yang configurations of heaven (historian Ulrike Unschuld translated this theory as describing a kind of “thermogenic nature”).

Similarly, the taste of drugs, also described in pharmacopeias but not systematized, became standardized in order to match the five phases that constituted the Earth. A coherent picture of the cosmos, combining heaven and Earth, thus encompassed endless combinations of those variables that in turn mapped on to different seasonal cycles and pharmacological actions. Employing this model, the master physician’s diagnosis and prescription thus became a complex process of reasoning that took everything into account: time, location, the site of the disease, the patient’s bodily constitution, and the nature of individual drugs (see table 1.1). In other words, to be a good physician was to read the hidden mechanisms of the macro- and microcosms like a diviner.
史家已对新宇宙论医学的创新之处及其深远遗产作了大量论述。

由于张元素、李杲及其弟子都生活在金朝统治下的北方，他们的宇宙论药学后来被记忆为一种北方现象。然而与张元素同时，南宋理学领袖朱熹（1130—1200）也对药性表现出浓厚兴趣。在朱熹与弟子的语录中（这些弟子通常并不学医），朱熹屡屡提及本草，以申明两个对其学说至关重要的论点。第一，药物虽呈“枯槁”之状，却绝非惰性物质，而是显然具有效力。在这个意义上，朱熹论及附子之性为热（能引起热感），大黄之性为“寒”。朱熹主张，这证明了人在其“性”中具有一种无形却强有力的道德判断能力。借由药性，朱熹指向了世界的一种更大“理”的存在。
Historians have written at length about the innovative aspects of this new cosmic medicine and its long-lasting legacy.

Since Zhang Yuansu, Li Gao, and their disciples all lived in the north under Jin rule, their cosmic pharmacy came to be remembered as a northern phenomenon. Yet contemporary to Zhang’s time, we also find Zhu Xi (1130–1200), a leading figure in Southern Song Confucianism, taking an active interest in the nature of drugs. In the recorded conversations between Zhu and his disciples (who were, in general, not training to practice medicine), Zhu Xi repeatedly brought up the topic of materia medica to make two claims important to his doctrine. First, despite their “withered and dried” (
kugao

) appearance, drugs were no inert matter, but obviously potent. In this sense, Zhu discussed the “nature” of aconite being hot (causing the sensation of heat) and that of rhubarb being “cold.” This, argued Zhu Xi, proves that human beings possess the invisible, but nevertheless potent, capacity of moral judgment in their “Nature” (
xing
). Through the nature of drugs, Zhu pointed to the existence of a greater coherence (
li
) of the world.

A second point derives from the first one in seemingly contradictory ways. While the nature of drugs could illuminate the moral nature of humanity, Zhu Xi sought to uphold a strict hierarchy between the high and the low, the grand and the minuscule. He dismissed the idea that one could know perfect truth from mere appearances—for example, by examining the dried herbs in a pharmacy. Zhu took great pains to explain that perfect coherence existed in this imperfect material world like a “bright pearl dropped into turbid water.”

For Zhu Xi, materiality prevented the full manifestation of this coherence, and he was only interested in the nature of drugs insofar as it helped him prove that coherence was indeed invisible and omnipresent. In chapter 3, we will revisit this influential doctrine and its critics in the seventeenth century.

这里的关键在于，北方与南方对宇宙论医学都有一致的兴趣，而这些新理论同时得到了医家与儒家士人的认可。沿着这一路向，13世纪后期出现了一部综合性论著，题为《汤液本草》，作者王好古（约活动于1264年）兼师张元素与李杲。张、李二人未曾试图以自己的学说取代本草药典，王好古却自信地把自己所传之学称作神农的“正学”。在序言中，王好古反对唐宋药典按矿物、植物、动物次序排列药物的分类体系，主张按照药性与药理作用部位讨论二三百种常用药。
1279年蒙古灭南宋后，张、李、王三家的刻本文集在蒙古统治下依然流行。可以说，在中国历史上，儒家士人与医学专家之间的互动，未曾有哪个时期比此时更密切、更互惠。

The important point here is that there existed a confluence of interest in cosmic medicine in both north and south, and that the new theories received endorsement by both physicians and Confucian literati. A synthetic treatise along these lines emerged in the late thirteenth century, titled
Tangye bencao (Materia medica for decoctions

) and authored by Wang Haogu (fl. 1264), a disciple of both Zhang Yuansu and Li Gao. Whereas Zhang and Li made no attempt to replace the bencao pharmacopeia with their own teachings, Wang felt confident to claim the “orthodox learning” (
zhengxue

) of the Divine Farmer in his own teachings. In his preface, Wang rejected the Tang and Song pharmacopeias’ classification system that sorted objects by the order of minerals, plants, and animals, proposing instead to discuss the 200–300 common drugs according to their nature and sites of pharmacological action.

Printed collections of Zhang, Li, and Wang remained popular under Mongol rule, after the latter vanquished the Southern Song in 1279. Arguably, during no other period in Chinese history had there been a closer, or more mutually beneficial, interaction between Confucian literati and medical experts.

那么，我们应当如何理解史家所称宋元明时期医学的这一胜利时刻？儒家之学与医学的汇流似乎是当日的主流叙事，以至于金元诸师的再传弟子朱震亨（1281—1358）声称，医学与儒家通过“格致”追求道德真理的事业本是一事。
在元朝蒙古统治下的华南，发展出一种独特的医学文化：“医户”与占星者（所谓阴阳家）一样，凭其世袭身份在地方行政中得到承认。最成功的医者吸引士人为之揄扬，建立起长久的家族声誉，甚至凭医术占据要职。尽管医户成员不能自由地与士人家族交往、通婚——他们“算不得十足的君子”——但他们在自身实践中借用儒家的辞令与礼仪，未必就是低人一等的表现。

How, then, should we understand this moment of triumph for medicine during what historians have called the Song-Yuan-Ming period? The confluence of Confucian and medical learning seemed to be the dominant narrative of the day, so much so that Zhu Zhenheng (1281–1358), a later disciple of the Jin-Yuan masters, claimed that medicine was one and the same with the Confucian pursuit of moral truth through the “investigation of things” (
gezhi
A unique medical culture developed in South China under the Mongol rulers of the Yuan dynasty, where “medical households” (
yihu
), along with astrologers (known as
yinyang

experts), were recognized by their hereditary status in local administrations. The most successful practitioners attracted literati advocates, established long-standing family reputations, and even occupied key governmental positions by virtue of their art. Even though members of the medical households could not freely mingle and intermarry with literati families—being “not quite gentleman”—their borrowing of Confucian tropes and rituals in their own practices was not necessarily a sign of inferiority.
1368年朱元璋击败蒙古人、建立明朝后，在朝中同时安置了大批技术专家与士人官员，并延续了聘用世袭医者充任各府县医学与惠民药局的惯例。我要说明的是，直到15世纪，行医者仍稳固地掌控着自身的技艺，其专家身份也得到了元朝与明初国家在制度上的承认。儒家哲人把医学及其他技术之艺视为宇宙论推理的来源，这反过来又在他们自己的思想中留下了不可磨灭的印记。

When Zhu Yuanzhang founded the Ming dynasty after defeating the Mongols in 1368, he staffed the court with a robust presence of technical experts along with scholar-officials and continued the practice of hiring hereditary physicians to staff local medical academies (
yixue

) and philanthropic pharmacies in every county seat. My point here is that, up to the fifteenth century, medical practitioners still possessed solid control over their art, and their status as experts received recognition institutionally by the Yuan and early Ming states. Confucian philosophers looked up to medicine and other technical arts as sources of cosmic reasoning, which in turn left indelible marks on their own thinking.
王履（1332—？）是这一时期一位有趣的博通之士。他画出过出色的山水画，据说还曾师从名医朱震亨学医。在其文集里，王履对本草的根本神话作了一句随口的评论：相传上古圣王神农尝百草，以分辨良药与毒物。然而在王履看来，一位圣王竟须把东西放进嘴里才能知道其性，这是不可思议的。他主张，本草的起源必定来自关于宇宙运行的神圣直觉之知（对王履而言，即《周易》的八卦），别无其他。
我们在此看到宇宙论医学的强大力量，它塑造了当日一般的认识论话语。直觉思维作为通向道德知识的重要渠道而兴起，正是以金元时期的理论性宇宙论医学为范本，其面貌始终深具神秘色彩。第三章我们将看到，对物质性与感官知识的敌意如何开始让位于一种更为肯定的态度，而这又影响了士人进入本草领域的方式。

Wang Lü (1332–?) represents an interesting polymath figure during this period. He composed excellent landscape paintings and reportedly studied medicine with the master physician Zhu Zhenheng. In his literary anthology, Wang made one off-handed remark about the foundational myth of bencao, in which the ancient sage-king Divine Farmer (
Shennong

) allegedly tasted one hundred herbs to tell good medicines from poison. Yet for Wang, it was inconceivable that a sage-king might have to put anything into his mouth in order to know its nature. He argued that the origin of bencao must instead be from divine intuitive knowledge about the workings of the cosmos (for Wang, the Eight Trigrams of the
Book of Changes
), and nothing else.

Here we see the compelling power of cosmic medicine that shaped the general epistemic discourses of the day. The rise of intuitive thinking as an essential conduit toward moral knowledge was modeled after the theoretical cosmic medicine of Jin-Yuan times and remained deeply mystical in its outlook. In chapter 3, we will return to see how the hostile attitude toward materiality and sensual knowledge began to give way to one more positive, which in turn impacted literati approaches to the field of bencao.

声望的去中心化：本草药典与明代官刻
Decentering Prestige: The Bencao Pharmacopeia and Ming Official Publishing
这段跨越数百年的简短旅程，如今把我们带回16世纪初。弘治皇帝对医学怀有浓厚兴趣，命刘文泰修订药典。自明朝开国以来，宫廷医官在朝中一直颇为显眼，尽管未必总受尊重。其中不少人声名之盛，足以使自己的传记载入正史。
我们现在更能理解，刘文泰受命编纂新药典时，为何希望它简明扼要——因为医学的最高学问本应如此。刘文泰在15世纪中叶经历医学学徒训练，应当熟悉金元主要学派的宇宙论药理学。此外，他也与东南商业书坊所刊行的一批药性“节要”与“粗浅注疏”处于同一时代，这些出版物相当独立于士人的意见。
这些作品或许启发他压缩药典中冗长的引文、重组内容，使之总体上更易阅读。

This brief journey through several centuries now brings us back to the early 1500s, when the Hongzhi emperor took a passionate interest in medicine and commissioned Liu Wentai to revise the pharmacopeia. Since the founding of the dynasty, Ming palace physicians had enjoyed visibility at court, if not always respect. Quite a few of them gained enough prominence in public life that their biographies appeared in the dynastic history.

We can now better understand why Liu Wentai, when charged with the task of making a new pharmacopeia, would have wanted to make it concise and simple, for this was how the highest learning in medicine was supposed to be. Going through his medical apprenticeship in the mid-fifteenth century, Liu would have been familiar with the leading Jin-Yuan schools of cosmic pharmacology. In addition, he was also contemporary to an array of “summaries” and “crude commentaries” on the nature of drugs published by commercial printing houses in the southeast, quite independent of literati opinions.
These works may have inspired him to condense the pharmacopeia’s verbose quotations and reorganize its content, making it more readable in general.

然而与此同时，刘文泰的政治对手也开始形成自己对本草的看法。自1249年平阳刻本以来两百多年间，宋代药典未曾刊行过重要新版本。这一局面直到1468年才改变：山东几位高级地方官员在济南按察司衙门赞助刊刻了一部新的《证类本草》（见地图0.1）。他们在序中解释说，1249年版的一部孤本出自山东一位下级官员的藏书，此人自称是在先前任职平阳时得到的。校勘、校对底本以及雕造总计1,340块版片的印制工程，在几位地方官吏与一位寓居士人的监督下如期完成。这部山东刻本请得内阁大学士商辂（1414—1486）作序，因而带有一种恢宏气度，使它与较廉价的坊刻区别开来。生动的插图与精雕的版片忠实保留了1249年版的许多特征（图1.1）。

At the same time, however, Liu Wentai’s political rivals also started to form their own opinions about bencao. For more than two centuries since the 1249 Pingyang edition, no major new edition of the Song pharmacopeia had been issued. The situation only changed in 1468, when a small number of high-ranking provincial officials of the Shandong Province sponsored a new edition of
Zhenglei bencao

at the Provincial Judge’s office in Jinan (map 0.1). In their prefaces, they explained that a lone copy of the 1249 edition had emerged from the collection of a lower-ranking official in Shandong, who said that he had acquired it during a previous post in Pingyang. The printing process, which involved collating and proofreading the existing copy, as well as the carving of a total of 1,340 woodblocks, was completed on schedule under the supervision of several local administrators together with one “sojourning literatus.” Graced by an invited preface from the grand secretariat Shang Lu (1414–86), the Shandong edition carries the air of magnanimity that distinguished it from the cheaper commercial imprints. The vivid illustrations and nicely carved blocks faithfully preserved many features of the 1249 edition (figure 1.1).
凭借山东刻本，唐慎微的本草在明代文化舞台上重获声名与声望，也为这部已有三百年历史的药典所载的日常细节添上了新的光彩。新任地方官员在1523、1552、1572与1624年多次下令重印并修补版片。一位省级监察官在1552年版的序中写道：“此书殆不可坐令其废。”

With the Shandong edition, Tang Shenwei’s bencao regained visibility and prestige on the Ming cultural scene, lending fresh luster to the mundane details recorded in the now three-hundred-year-old pharmacopeia. Newcomers to the provincial administration ordered numerous reprints and repair of woodblocks in the years 1523, 1552, 1572, and 1624. A provincial censor noted in his preface to the 1552 edition: “we simply cannot afford to sit here and let the book fall out of use.”

整个16世纪，官刻成为频繁往来于帝国的官员间的一种时尚活动，他们随身携带新印的书籍与手帕，作为雅致的礼物。
宋元时期，地方官学拥有田产，以田租收入刻书；明代法律却剥夺了地方官员用于此项目的经费。即便刊行地方志，也要求知县或知府逐案筹资。
本草药典在明中叶地方官署中的重新出现表明，官员确实把它视为一项能够提升自身文坛地位的声望工程。与地方官员类似，驻于各省要地的明代宗藩也积极参与刊刻各种著作的新版，其中包括宋代药典。在研究明代王府文化这一独特现象时，柯律格（Craig Clunas）指出，每一个新版本都复制并承载着“一种普遍德性的地方版本”。
在一个格外特殊的例子中，明代宗室朱橚（1361—1425）在华中开创性地编成了一种新的本草类型，只收录饥荒时可食的植物。朱橚的书仅载414种植物，篇幅短至两卷，显著地不涉医学旨趣。我们在此看到一种为政府用途而设计的“去医学化”本草的另类构想，这一路径在清代将赢得更多同情（见第四章）。

Throughout the sixteenth century, official publishing became a fashionable activity among officials who frequently traversed the empire, bringing newly printed books and handkerchiefs with them as elegant gifts.

Unlike the Song and Yuan periods, when local government academies owned land and used the revenue to publish books, Ming law deprived local officials of funding for that specific purpose. Even the publishing of local gazetteers (
difangzhi
) demanded that the magistrate or prefect raise funds on a case-by-case basis.

The reemergence of the bencao pharmacopeia in mid-Ming provincial administrations indicated that officials truly saw it as a prestige project that could boost their profile in the world of letters. Similar to the provincial officials, Ming princely households stationed in major provincial locations also actively participated in publishing new editions of different works, including the Song pharmacopeia. In his study of this unique phenomenon of Ming princely court culture, Craig Clunas remarked that each new edition reproduced carried “a local version of a universal virtue.”

In one extraordinary case, Zhu Su (1361–1425), a Ming prince in central China, conducted pathbreaking work to create a new genre of bencao that focused only on edible plants useful in times of famine. Containing only 414 plants and as short as two
juan

(volumes), Zhu Su’s text was remarkably devoid of medical interest. Here, we see an alternative vision for a de-medicalized bencao tailored for governmental purposes, an approach that would win greater sympathy in Qing times (see chapter 4).

总而言之，明代官员与宗藩的地方刊刻，无意中把本草药典的声望从朝廷下移到了地方。其结果是一幅极为分散却又彼此关联的知识传播图景：一部著名版本常常在别处被取用、翻刻。根据16世纪中叶一份关于各地出版的调查，宋代药典的各种版本以雕版（每套一千三百余块）的形式，见于北京与南京的国子监，以及南京、山东、广州乃至贵州的省、府衙门。
其中，山东刻本的历次重印影响最为持久。1581年，南京书业的大商家富春堂投资刊行一部精美的宋代药典，标榜“山东原板”并附有新特色。
更晚到17世纪，多产作家冯梦龙（1574—1646）在一篇短篇小说中利用了这层山东渊源。主人公是一位和蔼的老人，纯凭好运得到一剂神药，却向好奇的围观者吹嘘自己的医学学识。“那《大观本草》这部书，却不出在我山东的？”此人说道，尽管他对医学一窍不通。

Taken together, provincial publishing by Ming officials and princely courts unwittingly moved the prestige of bencao pharmacopeias away from the imperial court down to the localities. The result was a remarkably scattered yet mutually connected landscape of knowledge transmission, in which one famous edition was often taken up and reproduced elsewhere. According to a mid-sixteenth-century survey of regional publishing, various editions of the Song pharmacopeia, in the form of carved woodblocks (over 1,300 blocks in each set), were known to exist in the Beijing and Nanjing Imperial Academies, as well as the provincial and prefectural offices in Nanjing, Shandong, Guangzhou, and as far as Guizhou.
Among these, the consecutive reprints of the Shandong edition commanded the most enduring impact. In 1581,
Fuchuntang
(Hall of Wealth and Springtime), a major player in the Nanjing book market, invested in an elaborate edition of the Song pharmacopeia, advertising “original Shandong blocks” (
Shandong yuanban
) with new features.

Still later in the seventeenth century, the prolific author Feng Menglong (1574–1646) used the Shandong connection in one of his short stories. The protagonist—an affable old man who obtained a divine panacea by sheer good luck, boasted about his medical learning to curious spectators. “Can’t you see that the book of
Daguan bencao
in fact comes from Shandong, my home province?” says the man, in spite of his complete ignorance of medicine.
本草药典的地方化，可以从1575年刊行的两部有趣的宋代本草新版中看出。第一部出自北京内府，由年仅十二岁、三年前刚刚登基的万历皇帝下令制作。万历时版纯属宫廷工程，模仿流行的山东本草；皇帝的短序毫无邀请文官参与之意，万历也未尝试委派御医改进、修订书的内容。
换言之，1575年的帝国中心不过是在复制另一种“普遍德性的地方版本”，而不是体现并改进它。

The localization of bencao pharmacopeia can be seen from two interesting new editions of the Song bencao, both published in 1575. The first came from the Inner Court (
neifu

) in Beijing and was made by order of the twelve-year-old Wanli emperor, who had just ascended the throne three years prior. Solely a palace undertaking, the Wanli edition imitated the popular Shandong bencao, and the emperor’s short preface showed no interest in inviting the participation of civil officials, nor did Wanli attempt to commission imperial physicians to improve and revise the book’s content.
In other words, the imperial center in 1575 was merely reproducing another “local version of a universal virtue,” rather than embodying and improving it.

同年，另一部独特的宋代药典版本在南直隶南端的南陵县（见地图0.1）完成。制作费用高达三百两白银，在当时是一笔可观的数目——多数地方志大概是一县官署中最显眼的文化工程，刊刻费用却很少超过一百两（图1.2）。
南陵本引人注目之处在于，出资刊刻本草的并非地方官员，而是一位名叫王秋的富户。王秋以“坊市人”的身份长大，却以耿直而明达之名载入地方史。他的父亲曾捐谷赈饥，王秋也同样捐资修桥、资助需要衣食的贫寒学子。
王秋本人未受良好教育，但他的两个儿子通过了入学考试，成为地方学校的生员，并参与了新本草的筹备。赞助一部本草新版，很可能是王家以财富积累文化资本的又一关键步骤。

During the same year, another unique edition of the Song pharmacopeia was completed in Nanling, a county located at the southern edge of the southern metropolitan region (
nanzhili
, see map 0.1). The production cost ran as high as three hundred
liang

of silver, a considerable sum at the time, when most local gazetteers—likely the most high-profile cultural projects in an average county office—rarely cost more than 100 liang to produce (figure 1.2).
What was remarkable in the Nanling edition was that it was not the local officials who funded the printing of bencao, but a wealthy commoner named Wang Qiu. Growing up a “man of the marketplace” (
fangshiren

), Wang left his name in local histories as a “forthright and wise man.” His father had in the past donated grain for poor relief, and Wang Qiu similarly contributed to bridge repair and supported poor students who needed sustenance.

Although Wang Qiu himself lacked a good education, two of his sons passed the entry-level examinations and qualified as licentiates at the local academy, and they also participated in the preparation of the new bencao. The sponsoring of a new edition of bencao likely constituted another crucial step for the Wang family to accrue cultural capital with their wealth.

现代学者已指出南陵本宋代药典中的多处编辑错误，例如把一部旧版的牌记草率地移接到另一部书的正文之中。
他们的批评透露出一种挥之不去的意识：旧精英与新富之间存在着身份鸿沟。然而南陵本显然成了当时地方自豪感的来源。王氏兄弟在序中称赞父亲的节俭，声称“家无长物”。这位白手起家的“坊市人”的德行，使他得以从事更有教化意义的义举，包括刊行一部本草药典；王氏称其刊刻经费“前代皆以官帑充之”。
几十年后，一位本地知县用这副雕版重印新本，强调多亏王秋的慷慨，南陵终于有了自己的本草。
在这里，官刻与私刻的界限变得模糊，进一步强化了这样一种感觉：药典可以、也应当向任何关心公共福祉的人开放。

Modern scholars have noted multiple editorial errors in the Nanling edition of the Song pharmacopeia, such as the careless grafting of colophons from one previous edition to the main text of another.

Their critique revealed the lingering awareness of the status gap between the old elite and nouveau riche. Yet the Nanling edition clearly became a source of local pride at the time. In their preface, the Wang brothers praised their father’s frugality, claiming that they had “no superfluous things at home.” The virtue of the self-made “man of the marketplace” enabled him to pursue more edifying exploits, including making a bencao pharmacopeia that “had always been transmitted with official funds.”
A few decades later, a local magistrate used the carved woodblocks to publish a new reprint, emphasizing that thanks to Wang Qiu’s generosity, Nanling “finally has a bencao of our own.”
Here the boundary between official and private publishing came to be blurred, enhancing the sense that the pharmacopeia could and should be accessible to anyone interested in public welfare.

便携的宝藏：节要本草与商业出版
Portable Treasures: Abridged Bencao and Commercial Publishing
16世纪刊行的本草药典新版数量之大，使人们得以前所未有地接触这一文本。其结果是，越来越多的中层文本涌现出来，填补了《药性赋》一类启蒙读本与全本药典之间的空隙。作者们开始撰写在体例上稍为复杂的药学入门书，提供宋代药典的节要本。此类尝试无疑在唐宋时期便已开始，但到16世纪，更多作者被吸引来刊行自己的研读笔记，明确目标是以印刷文字博取个人名声。

The sheer quantity of new editions of bencao pharmacopeia produced during the sixteenth century offered unprecedented access to the text. As a result, a larger number of middle-range texts emerged that could bridge the gap between a primer text like
Rhymes

and a full-length pharmacopeia. Authors began to compose introductory pharmacy texts that were slightly more sophisticated in format, offering abridged versions of the Song pharmacopeia. Although such attempts had no doubt already started in the Tang and Song times, it was in the sixteenth century that more authors were attracted to publishing their study notes, with a clear goal of achieving personal fame through printed words.

第一部在印刷流通上取得成功的节要本草，是王纶（1484年进士）编纂的《本草集要》。王纶是一位资深文官，出身医学世家。他从宋代药典中选取545种药，把冗长的描述概括为短韵，从而在全本本草（约1,700种）与流行入门书（200—300种）之间找到了一条中间道路。王纶在序中批评药典“繁杂重复”，令读者不禁呵欠连连、昏昏欲睡，以此为自己的工作辩护。但他也对药典的权威表示恭顺，劝勉任何有志成为“专门之士”的认真学生研读“全书”。1510年与1529年又出两版，都相当成功。
The first major abridged bencao to succeed in print circulation was
Bencao jiyao (Summaries of Materia Medica
), compiled by Wang Lun (
jinshi

1484), a seasoned civil official with a family background in medicine. Picking a total of 545 drugs from the Song pharmacopeia and summarizing the long description into short verse, Wang Lun found a middle ground between the full bencao (~1,700) and popular primers (200–300). In his preface, Wang Lun justified his work by criticizing the “overly complex and repetitive” nature of the pharmacopeia, so much so that the reader could not help but yawn and feel drowsy. Yet he also spoke deferentially about the pharmacopeia’s authority, exhorting any serious student who aspired to become a “professional expert” (
zhuanmen zhi shi
) to study “the whole book.” Two more editions dated to 1510 and 1529 both enjoyed considerable success.
王纶的著作直接影响了至少两位同样在16世纪编纂节要本草的人。王机（1463—1539）与陈嘉谟（约活动于1565年）都是徽州府的成功医者，当地行医与出版业十分兴旺。
事实上，借印刷术成名的诱惑，很可能使他们产生了把医疗实践扩展为更大事业的想法。陈嘉谟尤其提到，学生们恳求他刊行自己的私授讲义，并径直把书题为《本草蒙筌》。陈嘉谟把药典中杂多的信息重新编排为悦目而对称的联句，便于朗读。此书尽管篇幅可观（约二十卷），读来却轻松流畅。

Wang’s work directly influenced at least two others who also composed abridged bencao in the sixteenth century. Both men, Wang Ji (1463–1539) and Chen Jiamo (fl. 1565), were successful physicians from Huizhou Prefecture, where medical practice and publishing flourished.

In fact, the lure of celebrity through print may well have given them the idea of expanding their medical practice into something much bigger. Chen Jiamo, in particular, noted how his students begged him to publish his private instructions and explicitly titled his book
Bencao mengquan (Instruments for Beginners in Materia Medica

). Chen rearranged the miscellaneous information in the pharmacopeia into pleasant and symmetrical couplets that were conducive to reading out aloud. Despite its considerable length (~20 volumes), the book is a breeze to read.

在漫长的万历朝（1572—1620），节要本很快进入不断扩张的商业出版领域。例如，陈嘉谟的本草既由福建历史悠久的医学书坊刊行，也由南都南京的新兴书坊刊行。
与此同时，地方志记载有些医者放弃行医，专注于著述这一“不朽业”。
节要本草比全本药典短，又比金元启蒙读物复杂，为有意著述者提供了一种理想体裁，可以同时吸引书商与读者。出版成功的诱惑也导致了剽窃，在某些情况下甚至公然伪造作者。这一时期出现了一部题为《本草约言》的短论，托名于薛己（1487—1559）——一位曾在太医院任职、后致仕居苏州的名医。学界现已公认，薛己本人不可能编成这部节要本草。
然而，一篇署薛己之名撰写的序言，仍雄辩地把本草之“约”说成一种博学工夫：

The abridged bencao quickly found their way into the expanding sector of commercial publishing during the long Wanli reign (1572–1620). Chen Jiamo’s bencao, for example, was published by both the long-standing medical publishing houses in Fujian and newer establishments in Nanjing, the southern capital.
Also at this time, local gazetteers recorded physicians giving up their practices to focus on the “immortal enterprise” (
buxiu ye
) of authorship.

Shorter than the full pharmacopeia yet more elaborate than the Jin-Yuan primers, the abridged bencao offered an ideal genre with which prospective authors could appeal to both publishers and readers. The appeal of publishing success also resulted in plagiarism and, in certain cases, blatant fabrication of authorship in published texts. A short treatise titled
Bencao yueyan (Concise Discourse on Materia Medica

) emerged during this period and was attributed to Xue Ji (1487–1559), a highly successful physician who served in the Imperial Academy of Medicine and retired to Suzhou. Scholars now agree that Xue Ji himself could not have composed this abridged bencao.
Yet a preface written under Xue’s name nevertheless spoke eloquently to the abridgement (
yue
) of bencao as a learned exercise:
“余生也晚，幸秘笈无不发之藏，故余得游息其间，积有年所。时就本草中，辑其日用不可缺者，分为二种〔药用、食疗〕，且别以类，志约也。韦编几绝，丹黄斑驳不复识。”

I was born in a later age. Fortunately, all secret texts have been uncovered from their depositories, so I was able to dwell there for many years. I kept compiling indispensable and frequently used drugs from
bencao

, grouped them into two categories [medicinal and dietetic], and classified them by their kinds, so that the account was concise. [In doing so] my book bindings wore out several times; my notes in red ink and corrections in yellow ink covered the whole page to the extent it became illegible.
序言接着许诺一种愉悦的阅读体验：
The preface goes on to promise a pleasant reading experience:
“因思神农生人之泽，昭垂万祀，而全本浩汗难竟，则斯帙也，其径捷，其功逸，其神不劳。寓目之余，条分缕指，无不备具。所谓开卷一读，生气满堂者，其在斯乎。”

I thought of the Divine Farmer’s profound offerings to the benefit of mankind, which is going to be the model for ten thousand generations. However, the complete book was so vast that one might never reach its end. As for this present volume, the path is short, the effort is easy, and the reader’s mind will not be exhausted. At a glance, all the entries and details are presented clearly and in a comprehensive way. This is the kind of book that will enliven your room just by opening it.
“案头箧际，可披可携”，《约言》以一条通往“知识的秘藏”的易行之路迎合通俗读者。对晚明读者而言，作者身份的真伪，不如书中公开许诺的轻松获取有用知识来得重要。弘治药典的不幸，或许并不在于其编者被指控的道德过失，而在于其形式的专属性：作为一部精美写本，它无法与明代各地大量涌现的印本本草所造成的影响相抗衡。
“On the desk or in the suitcase, readable and portable,”
Concise Discourses

catered to the popular reader by offering an easy path into the “secret deposits of knowledge.” The authenticity of authorship mattered less to late Ming readers than the open promise of acquiring useful knowledge without much effort. Perhaps the misfortune of the Hongzhi pharmacopeia lies not in the putative moral failings of its editor, but rather the exclusiveness of its format: as an exquisite manuscript, it could not compete with the impact made by the proliferating number of bencao texts coming in print from multiple loci of the Ming realm.

节要本草作为一种体面而实用的体裁兴起，也引起了当时名医的注意。1570年代，太医院高官、北京一个颇具影响力的医会（yihui）领袖徐春甫（1520—1596）借助印刷文字传播正统医学教说。一部展示徐春甫博学的长篇汇编《古今医统大全》在徽州府获得了热烈的刊行支持。然而，本草这一主题在全书中出现得相当晚（一百卷中的第七十一卷），内容也只是照录王纶的节要本草。在书中其他地方，徐春甫指出，医者最重要的是正确诊断疾病的能力，诊断既明，准确的治法自然随之而来。
在此，徐春甫借用王纶的文本以示认可，同时也试图把节要本草纳入“医宗”的结构之下。第三章我们将看到，业余士人与正统医者之间围绕药学之学的这一张力，如何在17世纪公开爆发。

The rise of abridged bencao as a respectable and practical genre did not escape the attention of leading physicians of the day. In the 1570s, Xu Chunfu (1520–96), a high-ranking member of the Imperial Academy of Medicine and leader of an influential medical association (
yihui
) in Beijing, took to the printed word to spread authentic medical teaching. A long compendium that showcased Xu’s erudition,
Complete Collection on Medical Orthodoxy in Ancient and Modern Times (Gujin yitong daquan
), received enthusiastic support for publication in Huizhou Prefecture. The subject of bencao, however, only appears quite late in the volume (the seventy-first of a hundred
juan

, or fascicles), and the content simply reproduced Wang Lun’s abridged bencao. Elsewhere in the work, Xu indicates that the most important thing for a physician was the capacity to correctly diagnose diseases, and once that is achieved, accurate therapeutics would naturally follow.
Here, Xu borrowed Wang’s text in a gesture of approval yet also sought to contain the abridged bencao under the structure of a “medical orthodoxy” (
yizong
). In chapter 3, we will see how this tension between amateur literati and orthodox physicians over pharmacological learning later broke into the open in the seventeenth century.

食疗本草、雷公文本与私人财富
Dietetic Bencao, Master Thunder Texts, and Private Wealth

晚明书籍文化大力推动的另一类本草写作是食疗论著，即从包罗万象的药典中择取材料、专论食物药性的文本。明代博学读者知道，以饮食疗病在古代礼书中已作为一种独立的医术出现，而饮食调养之论也被纳入唐宋药典。后来在蒙古统治下，元朝宫廷促成了中原与中亚饮食、医学传统的融合。回回宫廷医官忽思慧（约活动于1330年）编纂了一部卷帙宏富的宫廷饮食谱（即《饮膳正要》），配有描绘宫廷食物制作过程的丰富插图。此书在明代由宦官机构重刻，一直颇为流行。

Another genre of bencao writing that received a great boost from late Ming book culture was dietetic treatises, or texts that focused on the medicinal properties of foods by selectively drawing from the all-encompassing pharmacopeia. Learned readers in Ming China knew that healing through diet had appeared in ancient ritual texts as a separate medical expertise, and that treatises on dietetic advice were incorporated into the Tang and Song pharmacopeias. Later, under Mongol rule, the Yuan court brought forth a fusion of Chinese and Central Asian dietary and medical traditions. Husihui (fl. 1330), a Muslim palace physician, compiled an extensive collection of culinary recipes with rich illustrations of the preparation of food at court. His work was reprinted during the Ming by the eunuch administration and remained popular.
同样在蒙古统治末期（14世纪初），南方的中国士人开始从宋代药典中摘录有用的食疗条目。其成果通常为四至八卷的短小便携手册，以《日用本草》一类书名流传。16世纪，多种食疗本草印本问世，作者（及改编者）署名各不相同，多为在州县任职但并不行医的士大夫。他们的著作迎合了士人阶层日益增长的自养需求，城市书商则抓住这一需求，制作更易消化的文本，往往附有可疑的作者署名。
与上一节所论至少仍声称有助于医学训练的节要本草相比，“日用”类食疗本草更明确地以有余力、或向往精致生活的业余读者为对象。

Also toward the end of Mongol rule (the early fourteenth century), Chinese literati in the south started excerpting useful tidbits of dietetic medicine from the Song pharmacopeia. The result (usually short, portable manuals of four to eight volumes) was transmitted under titles such as
Bencao for Everyday Use (Riyong bencao

). During the sixteenth century, multiple versions of dietetic bencao appeared in print with varying attributions to different authors (and adaptors), mostly scholar-officials who held office at the district or prefectural level but were not medical practitioners. Their writings catered to the rising demand for self-care techniques among the literati class at large, and urban publishers seized on this demand, producing more easily digestible texts, often with dubious claims to authorship.

In comparison to the abridged bencao texts discussed in the previous section, which at least still claimed to facilitate medical training, the “everyday” dietetic bencao more explicitly targeted amateur readers who could afford, or aspired to, a refined lifestyle.

精英对一个技术性主题的兴趣日增，无论起初显得多么业余，都有助于提升该主题的公认地位。食品制作大概从来无法与药材的亲手炮制完全分开，而后者直到16世纪仍是由专家掌控的领域（详见第四章）。因此相当值得注意的是，大约在1580年代至1590年代间，福建、江西与南京的商业书坊刊行了一系列本草文本，前所未有地聚焦于生药材的加工。它们有别于金元短篇启蒙书与中型节要本草，收录的药物数量很大（900至1,200种，几乎与全本药典相当），篇幅却短得多（八卷）。与其他商业刊本一样，这些以制药为导向的本草有着冗长而繁复的书名；这里我称它们为“雷公”文本，因为这类书名通常含有“雷公”二字，把“炮制”之术系于一位姓雷（意为“雷”）的中古早期传统作者。

Heightened elite interest in a technical subject, however amateurish it may have appeared at first, helped raise the perceived status of the subject matter. The preparation of foodstuffs is arguably never fully distinguishable from the hands-on preparation of materia medica, a domain controlled by experts well into the sixteenth century (more on this in chapter 4). It is thus quite remarkable that roughly between the 1580s and 1590s, commercial publishers in Fujian, Jiangxi, and Nanjing produced a series of bencao texts with an unprecedented focus on the processing of raw pharmaceutical substances. Distinct from the Jin-Yuan short primers and the midsized, abridged bencao, these texts covered a great number of substances (900–1,200 drugs, almost on the same scale of the full pharmacopeia) but managed to stay much shorter (8 volumes). Like other commercially published texts, these pharmaceutically oriented bencao had long and elaborate titles; here I refer to them as “Master Thunder” texts, after the common titular element that attributed the art of “roasting and preparation” (
paozhi
) to an early medieval tradition with an author surnamed Lei (meaning “thunder”).
那么，雷公究竟教了什么？这一传统又是如何进入本草药典的？学界现已公认，一部题为《雷公炮炙论》的著作可系于5世纪一位名叫雷斅的作者（大概是道教术士），其书又在10世纪经过编订与注释。
雷公的主体内容是关于如何使用约300种常用药的说明。书前有一篇托名雷斅的序，铺陈出一幅令人目眩的感应巫术与神效疗愈图景：用干鲑鱼触碰树木，树便会枯萎；把狗胆汁洒在将死的树上，树会复苏。雄鼠骨粉能使脱落的牙齿再生；半夏汁能使麻风病人保住头发与眉毛。11世纪后期，唐慎微决定把它收入自己扩充的本草，此后的刻本中也一直保留。

So what did Master Thunder teach, and how did this tradition find its way into the bencao pharmacopeia? Scholars now agree that a treatise known as
Master Thunder’s Discourse on Pharmaceuticals (Leigong paozhi lun
) can be dated to a fifth-century author (probably a Daoist adept) named Lei Xiao, whose work was in turn edited and glossed in the tenth century.
The main body of
Master Thunder
consisted of instructions on how to deploy (
shi

) about 300 common drugs. It has a preface attributed to Lei Xiao, presenting a dazzling display of sympathetic magic and miraculous cures: touch a tree with dried salmon and it will wither; sprinkling a dog’s bile juice on the dying tree would make it bounce back to life. The bone powder of a male rat makes fallen teeth grow again; the juice of the
banxia

plant helps lepers retain their hair and eyebrows. In the late eleventh century, Tang Shenwei decided to incorporate it into his expanded bencao, and it remained there in the subsequent print editions.

探究雷公何以在12世纪奇迹般兴起的具体历史情境，超出了本研究的范围。不过，我们可以从宋代博学之士如沈括（1031—1095）以及后来洪迈（1123—1202）把它引为可信证据的方式中找到线索；这反过来表明，宇宙感应及其在各种秘术中的神奇显现，曾深深吸引博学的士人。
It is beyond the scope of this study to inquire into the specific historical circumstances that enabled
Master Thunder

’s remarkable rise in the twelfth century. Yet we can find clues from the ways in which Song polymath scholars such as Shen Gua (1031–95) and later Hong Mai (1123–1202) cited it as credible evidence, which in turn suggests that cosmic resonance, along with its magical manifestations in various esoteric arts, deeply interested the learned literati.
换言之，理学思想的形成阶段，建立在一种对玄秘之事的根深蒂固的迷恋之上，也建立在一种乐观信念之上：无法解释的现象归根结底与世界的“理”本为一体。
然而，没有哪位宋代作者试图以理性语言阐明雷公，他们满足于让文本自己说话。晚明对雷公兴趣的复兴，恰与本草文本前所未有的普及同时发生，促成了一种凸显药学力量的新话语。

The formative stage of neo-Confucian thought was, in other words, built upon a deep-seated fascination with the occult and an optimism that unexplainable phenomena were fundamentally at one with the coherence (
li
) of the world.
Yet no Song authors attempted to elucidate
Master Thunder
on rational terms, content to let the text speak for itself. The late Ming resurgence of interest in
Master Thunder
coincided with unprecedented popularization of bencao texts, giving rise to a new discourse that highlighted the power of pharmacy.

细加考察便可发现，晚明的雷公文本其实是宋代药典摘录的拼合。其收载范围无疑比常见的启蒙读本宽泛，因为它们确实讨论了许多与日常医疗无关的秘异药物。与此同时，每条内容都被削减到最基本的要点，没有繁复的引文或图像。每篇中最详备的部分，是描述把原料转化为成品的制药过程。除了抄录药典，这些文本还包含概括各药要点的简短韵语，很可能是新撰的。在一些刻本中，韵语赫然置于每页的上栏。简言之，雷公文本的作者与出版者大多出身比食疗本草作者更为寒微，他们并非不加思索地拼凑旧文，而是有意借此机会推广自己在通俗药学方面的教说。
Examined closely, the late Ming
Master Thunder

texts turn out to be an amalgam of excerpts from the Song pharmacopeia. Their scope is definitely wider than the commonly seen primer texts, for they did discuss many esoteric substances not relevant for everyday medical practice. At the same time, each entry is stripped down to the bare essentials, devoid of elaborate quotations or pictures. The most elaborate section in each describes the pharmaceutical processes that turn raw material into a processed form. In addition to copying from the pharmacopeia, these texts include simple, short rhymes that summarize important facts about each drug and were likely to have been newly composed. In some printed editions, the rhymes are featured prominently on the top panels of each page. In short, the authors and publishers of Master Thunder texts, most of whom hailed from humbler backgrounds than dietetic bencao authors, did not thoughtlessly graft material from previous texts, but they also deliberately used the occasion to promote their own teachings in popular pharmacy.
最近发现的一部16世纪后期雷公文本写本，为了解当时复杂的读者问题提供了线索。写本明确署有1591年的日期，从其外观与书法风格看，与刘文泰那部命运多舛的16世纪初本草十分相似。学者推测，这部写本很可能出自宫廷画师之手：他们得到一部1587年刊行的雷公文本印本，大概奉万历皇帝之命，制作了这部图文富丽的副本。
同样值得注意的是，外朝文官并未参与制作，而写本一直藏在宫廷收藏中，直到20世纪。除了描绘九百余种药物，写本还以整页图幅呈现雷公所传的制药过程。卷首图绘一位身着华丽紫金袍的君子，主持着一处理想化的工作场所。九名工匠手持各种切、洗、炮制生药的器具围绕四周，这位大师看上去睿智而从容（见图1.3）。
A recent discovery of a manuscript of one late sixteenth-century
Master Thunder

text sheds light on the complex question of readership at the time. The manuscript has a clear date of 1591 and, judging by its appearance and calligraphic style, closely resembles Liu Wentai’s ill-fated early sixteenth-century bencao. Scholars have speculated that this manuscript was most likely the work of painters at court, who obtained a printed
Master Thunder
text released in 1587 and produced this richly illustrated copy, probably based on the Wanli emperor’s demand.

Again, it is notable that no civil officials of the outer court was involved in the production, and the manuscript remained in palace collection till the twentieth century. Aside from the portrayal of over 900 materia medica, the manuscript also featured full-page depictions of the pharmaceutical processes taught by Master Thunder. The opening image depicts a gentleman wearing an elaborate purple and golden robe, who presides over an idealized workspace. Surrounded by nine artisans wielding various tools for cutting, rinsing, and preparing raw medicines, the master looks wise and at ease with himself (see figure 1.3).

要阐明这些精美图像所运用的图像志与叙事手法，尚需更多研究。这里，中心与地方、公与私的界限，再次因人们对制药过程的共同迷恋而变得模糊。到16世纪最后几十年，商业刊行的雷公文本几乎开始盖过宋代药典那张博学而严肃的面孔，甚至引来了皇家的模仿。

More research is needed to elucidate the iconographic and narrative approaches employed in these elaborate images. Here again, the boundary between center and local, as well as between public and private, came to be blurred by virtue of a shared fascination with the pharmaceutical processes. Toward the last decades of the sixteenth century, commercially published
Master Thunder
texts almost started to overshadow the scholarly, stern face of the Song pharmacopeia, to the extent of inspiring imperial imitations.

从更广阔的视角看，雷公文本在晚明社会中的复兴，也是一种包容性的“养生”文化的组成部分；旧精英与新精英——包括明代皇室、贵族、精英士人与暴发户——都对此怀有热切的兴趣。这批文本颂扬制药的转化之力，既赞美工匠的劳动，也赞美这项工作的神明守护者。图像与文字凸显制药过程的物质性，唤起人们对物质效力与人心创造力的注意，并许诺把人从一切尘世烦忧中解救出来。雷公传统的古奥文辞掺入道教炼丹术的迷狂语言，更强化了这一许诺。最终，雷公文本偏离了旧本草文献兼收并蓄的路向，以对效验的狂热许诺取代了学者的审思。
Seen from an even broader perspective, the revival of
Master Thunder

texts in late Ming society was also part of an inclusive “nourishing life” culture, in which the old and new elite—including the Ming imperial family, aristocrats, elite literati, and the nouveau riche—all took an avid interest. By celebrating the transformative power of pharmaceutical processing, this body of texts praised artisanal labor as well as the godly patron of that work. Foregrounding the materiality of pharmaceutical processes, the pictures and texts call attention to the potency of matter and inventiveness of the human mind, with the promise to deliver men from all mundane worries. The archaic prose of the
Master Thunder
tradition intensified this promise by blending in the ecstatic language of Daoist alchemy. In the end, the
Master Thunder
texts deviated from the eclectic approach of the old bencao literature, substituting scholarly deliberation with rapturous promises of efficacy.
这就是李时珍在1580年代至1590年代反复为新药典寻求赞助时将学到的教训——这部药典完全由他一人编成。
This is the lesson that Li Shizhen would learn in the 1580s and 1590s, as he searched repeatedly for patronage for a new pharmacopeia that he had compiled all by himself.
刊行《本草纲目》：李时珍的策略
Publishing
Bencao gangmu
: Li Shizhen’s Strategies

李时珍（1518—1593）出生于湖广省蕲州一位医者之家。蕲州是一座依傍长江北岸的山城（见地图0.1）。李时珍自幼既受经典教育，也习医学，科举却屡屡不利，年纪轻轻便以医成名。三十多岁时，他进入楚王府，掌管王府宗庙的祭祀。1566年，李时珍被推荐到北京太医院任职，数年后致仕返回蕲州。其时，他的儿子李建元在科举上更为成功，已赴四川出任知县，也提升了父亲的社会地位。回乡后，李时珍得以新建宅第，坐拥湖景，与地方士绅交游，谈论医事与文章。

Li Shizhen (1518–93) was born the son of a physician living in the Qizhou Subprefecture of the Huguang Province, a mountainous town perched on the northern shore of the Yangzi River (map 0.1). Having received a classical education alongside medical training, Li had little luck in the civil examination but started earning his own reputation as a young physician. In his thirties, Li joined the court of Prince Chu and was put in charge of sacrifices at the prince’s ancestral shrine. In 1566, Li Shizhen was recommended to serve in the Imperial Academy of Medicine in Beijing, where he stayed for several years before retiring to Qizhou. By that time, Li’s own son Jianyuan had achieved more success in the civil examinations and gone off to Sichuan to serve as a county magistrate, raising the social status of his father as well. Back home, Li Shizhen was able to build a new residence with scenic views of a lake, where he socialized with local gentry and conversed about medical and literary matters.

然而安稳的生活与地方声望并未使李时珍满足。他怀有更大的目标：通过为更广泛的读者写作，巩固自己——以及父亲——的医学资历。1578年，李时珍刊行了两部脉法论著，其中对针法中素称难明的“奇经”作了详尽解释。他的一位士人朋友撰写了赞誉性的序言，这些著作在他本省付梓。
此外，李时珍还宣布完成了一部将取代宋代药典的新本草——一部宏伟的总汇，汇集关于1,892种药物的一切已知信息，前后耗费二十七年。1580年，李时珍携《本草纲目》稿本顺流而下，前往江南。要刊行此书，他需要本省圈子之外的推荐。

A secure life and local fame, however, did not make Li content. He harbored the greater goal of cementing his—and his father’s—medical credentials by writing for a broader audience. In 1578, Li published his first two treatises on the method of pulse diagnosis, featuring a thorough explanation of the so-called irregular conduits (
qijing
) that were notoriously difficult to grasp in needling. One of his literati friends wrote a flattering preface, and the works were printed in his home province.

In addition to that, Li announced the completion of a new bencao that would replace the Song pharmacopeia—a grand compendium containing all known information about 1,892 drugs that he had spent twenty-seven years to prepare. In 1580, Li sailed downstream with the manuscript of
Bencao gangmu
and headed for Jiangnan. To publish it, he needed endorsement from someone beyond his provincial circles.

李时珍此行的目的，是求见王世贞（1526—1590）。王世贞是一位暂时致仕的士大夫，闲居苏州府中的豪华别业。凭借极高的文名与广泛的人脉，王世贞足以成就或断送一个人的政治、文学生涯，因此他的居所门庭若市，访客络绎不绝。据王世贞自己回忆，比他年长八岁的李时珍显得略有几分局促，格格不入。两人相见之日，昙阳子——一位被王世贞奉为观世音菩萨活弟子的女教首——刚刚在一场众目睽睽的仪式中结束了自己的生命，在包括王世贞在内的许多显贵见证下“升天”；王世贞还写下狂喜的诗篇以纪其事。
王世贞当时思绪未定，便匆匆写下另一首诗赠李时珍，诗中温和地嘲弄了这位老人的认真：李时珍错在花了如此长的时间编纂本草；若非如此，他早已飞升仙界了。

The purpose of Li’s visit was to seek a meeting with Wang Shizhen (1526– 90), a scholar-official in temporary retirement at his lavish estate in the Suzhou Prefecture. With his towering literary fame and widespread connections, Wang could make or break one’s political or literary career, and, as a result, his residence teemed with visitors from near and far. In Wang’s own recollection, Li, who was eight years his elder, stood out as slightly awkward and out of place. On the day the two met, Tanyangzi, a female cult-leader whom Wang worshiped as living disciple of the Bodhisattva Guanyin, had just ended her own life in a public spectacle where she “ascended to the heaven” in front of many illustrious witnesses, including Wang Shizhen, who wrote rapturous poems to mark the occasion.

His thoughts were still preoccupied when he dashed off another poem to honor Li Shizhen, in which he gently mocked the seriousness of the old man: Li was wrong to have spent such a long time composing the bencao. Had that not been the case, he could have ascended to the realm of immortals long ago.

李时珍寻求士林领袖推荐的策略奏效了。初次相见十年后，李时珍再度拜访，终于得到王世贞的一篇短序，这或许促使南京一位小书商投资刊刻这部昂贵的新书。1593年，李时珍在南京去世，享年七十六岁。他的子孙设法在1596年完成了《本草纲目》的首次刻本。此后不久，李氏家族得知，京师的礼部正在征集对各类主题“成一家名言”的新近著作，以备编纂国史艺文志。1596年末，李时珍的一个儿子携书进京，同时呈上以父亲名义撰写的遗表。第二次争取皇家赞助的结果并不理想：朝廷只批了一句短语：“书留览，礼部知道。”三年后，明宫失火，史馆的征书工作中止。
没有证据表明李时珍的本草曾得到万历皇帝本人的垂注。

Li Shizhen’s strategy of seeking leading literati endorsement was successful. Ten years after their first meeting, Li finally obtained a short preface from Wang upon a second visit, which may have nudged a minor publisher in Nanjing to invest in this new and expensive text. In 1593, Li Shizhen passed away at the age of seventy-six in Nanjing. His sons and grandsons saw to it that the first print edition of
Bencao gangmu
was completed in 1596. Soon after that, the Li family learned that the Ministry of Rites in the imperial capital was soliciting submissions of recent books that “offered a unique opinion” (
cheng yijia zhi yan

) on any subject matter, in preparation for compiling a general bibliography for the dynastic history. In late 1596, a son of Li Shizhen traveled to Beijing with the book, along with a posthumous memorial to the Ming emperor written in his father’s name. The second attempt to acquire imperial patronage ended less well: the court only replied with a short note: “Keep the book for perusal; inform the Board of Rites.” Three years later, a fire broke out in the Ming palaces and the historiographical office’s book collecting came to a halt.
No evidence indicated that Li’s bencao received the Wanli emperor’s personal attention.

于是，我们拥有关于李时珍及其本草的两份非常不同的总体叙述：王世贞1590年的序，以及1596年李氏家族呈给御前的遗表。王世贞在序中一本正经地称赞李时珍的本草，却又试图淡化此书的医学意义。相反，他特别表彰书中展现的博学，认为它尤其有助于儒家对“物”“性”“理”之知的追求。此外，王世贞还展示了自己驾驭文字的独门本领，写出一联联缀满奇妙典故、宛如贯珠的对句。这篇序确实透露出当时在野士人与医者之间存在某种“共同的思想承诺”，但我们须小心，不可高估这两个迥然不同的人之间的协同与投契。
更准确的说法或许是，王世贞在李时珍的著作中发现了一座宝库，它照亮了王氏本人对物质效力、方术与长生超脱的迷恋。王世贞以无所不能的文化仲裁者自居，从未真正把李时珍视为与自己平等的人，也未曾认真看待他的医学训练。

We thus have two very different general accounts of Li Shizhen and his bencao: Wang Shizhen’s 1590 preface, as well as the posthumous memorial presented by the Li family to the throne in 1596. In his preface, Wang Shizhen praised Li’s bencao in all seriousness, but also sought to downplay the medical relevance of the work. Instead, Wang singled out the erudition displayed in its pages as particularly useful for the Confucian pursuit of the knowledge of things (
wu
), nature (
xing
), and coherence (
li

). In addition, Wang displayed his special knack for words, churning out couplets loaded with marvelous allusions like strings of pearls. While the preface did reveal the existence of some “common intellectual commitment” between lay literati and men of medicine at the time, we must be careful not to overestimate the synergy and rapport between the two very different individuals.

It may be more accurate to say that Wang saw a treasure trove in Li’s work, which illuminated the former’s own fascination with the potency of matter, magic, and immortal transcendence. Posing as the all-powerful arbiter of culture, Wang never truly considered Li his equal, nor took his medical training very seriously.

呈给御前的遗表则呈现出关于李时珍及其本草的另一种叙事。李时珍很可能在生前亲自起草了遗表正文，至少也在确定最终措辞时发挥了主要作用。在遗表中，李时珍对本草药典作了冗长而详细的陈述，把它描述为一种承载权威与庄严的体裁，一部“司命”于民的书。他还坦言，自己因以王府末吏的身份承担此事而怀有“僭著述之权”的惶恐。显然，在李时珍心中，《本草纲目》是一项公共善业，未必与士人文化相合。有趣的是，他似乎误解了五百年前同样参与药典编纂的宋代医者唐慎微。两人都是在远离主要文化中心的地区行医的医生，也都在没有正式官职的情况下完成了修订、扩充官方药典的非凡事业。然而李时珍坚称，北宋朝廷曾“命”唐慎微从事这项工作。在本草正文中，李时珍又断言唐慎微“上之朝廷”。或许李时珍希望，以这种方式叙述本草的历史，明廷也会赐予他的药典一种《证类本草》曾从宋帝那里获得的经典地位。

The posthumous memorial to the throne presents an altogether different narrative of Li Shizhen and his bencao. It is quite likely that Li Shizhen personally drafted the main text of the memorial before he died, or at least played a major role in shaping the final wording of the text. In the memorial, Li presented a long and detailed account of the bencao pharmacopeia, describing it as a genre invested with authority and gravitas, a book that “governed the destiny” (
siming
) of the people. He also confessed that he felt some trepidation over “usurping the power of composition” (
jian zhushu zhi quan
), as he had undertaken the task as only a former minor official in a princely court. It is evident that, in Li’s mind, he saw
Bencao gangmu

as a project of public good not necessarily congruent with literati culture. Interestingly, he seems to have misunderstood Tang Shenwei, the Song physician who also participated in pharmacopeia-making five centuries before him. Both were physi- cians practicing in places relatively remote from major cultural centers; both men achieved the extraordinary task of revising and expanding the official pharmacopeia without a formal role in government. Yet Li insisted that the Northern Song court had commissioned (
ming
) Tang Shenwei to work on the project. In the main text of his bencao, Li again asserted that Tang “presented his book to the court” (
shang zhi chaoting
). Perhaps Li hoped that by framing the history of bencao this way, the Ming court would also grant his pharmacopeia the canonical status that
Zhenglei bencao
had earned from the Song emperor.

两份叙述中，李时珍最一贯的特征是他对书籍的深挚热爱。王世贞嘲笑他的书痴，李时珍自己也承认读书“若啖蔗饴”。两份叙述都归结于他通过出版与著述对“不朽”的狂热追求。然而最终，李时珍既未从王世贞作序的南京本、也未从明廷那里获得他所期望的名声。1603年，江西巡抚（正二品）夏良心（1571年进士）得到一部《本草纲目》。夏良心曾在山东任职，大概熟悉当地官刻宋代药典之事。他以自身健康问题为由，热情推荐这部新本草，很快便从同僚处筹得足够资金，在江西省城刊行了一个全新版本。在两员下级官员的监督下，全部雕版与印刷仅用六个月便告完成（首版则准备了三年多），工艺质量也更高。
所谓江西本广为流布，很快促使李时珍的家乡湖广省赞助刊行了类似的版本。

The most consistent feature of Li Shizhen as portrayed in the two accounts lies in his deep love of books. Wang Shizhen mocked Li’s bookishness, and Li himself confessed to reading books “like craving sugar canes and candies.” The two accounts converged on his avid pursuit of “immortality” (
buxiu

) through publishing and authorship. In the end, however, Li Shizhen achieved the fame he hoped for neither from the Wang Shizhen-endorsed Nanjing edition nor from the Ming throne. In 1603, Xia Liangxin (jinshi 1571), grand coordinator (
xunfu
, rank 2a) of the Jiangxi Province, obtained a copy of
Bencao gangmu

. Having served in the Shandong provincial administration, Xia was probably familiar with the official publishing of the Song pharmacopeia there. Citing his own personal health issues, Xia recommended the new bencao with enthusiasm, and soon raised enough funds from colleagues to create a brand-new edition in the provincial capital of Jiangxi. With the supervision of two lower-ranking officials, all carving and printing were completed in only six months (compared to more than three years of preparation for the first edition), and with a higher quality of craftsmanship.
The so-called Jiangxi edition was widely distributed, quickly inspiring Huguang, Li Shizhen’s home province, to sponsor a similar edition.

帝国中国最后一部伟大的药典——一部英勇地以知识集中化为目标的文本——竟要依靠当时文化去中心化的潮流才得以成功，这或许是个悖论。李时珍梦想着一种由皇权维护、绵延不绝的本草传统，文人与医学专家在其中无缝合作。然而这并未实现。中央政府不仅不再控制本草文本的生产、流传与评判，还在物质资源的支配上面临日益激烈的挑战。在《本草纲目》江西本的序中，地方官员夏良心解释说，一切本草药典的核心都在于为民谋福的仁善目的。这种民本主义语调，与夏良心此前直言批评朝廷税收政策、主张减少对地方经济集中控制的记录正相吻合。
下一章我们将看到，药物之物如何在16世纪的国家治理与士大夫的积极行动中占据一席之地。无论文本还是物质商品，中心都将无法维持其控制。

It is perhaps paradoxical that imperial China’s last great pharmacopeia—a text that heroically aimed at centralizing knowledge—owed its success to the decentralizing cultural trends of the day. Li Shizhen dreamed of an unbroken bencao tradition upheld by imperial authority, under which men of letters collaborated seamlessly with medical experts. Yet this was not to be. Not only was the central government no longer in control of the production, transmission, and assessment of bencao texts, it also faced more vocal challenges over its disposal of material resources. In his preface to the Jiangxi edition of
Bencao gangmu

, the provincial official Xia Liangxin explained that at the heart of all bencao pharmacopeia lies a charitable purpose for the benefit of the people. The populist overtone fits well with Xia’s previous record as an outspoken critic of the court’s taxation policy and advocate for less centralized control over the local economy.

In the next chapter, we will see how pharmaceutical objects were featured in statecraft and scholar-official activism in the sixteenth century. The center will not hold in the control of both texts and material goods.
